enrichment.short_title: Asylum appeal on Article 8 expulsion to Czech Republic
key_facts: A Czech Roma woman claimed asylum in the UK citing persecution for her ethnicity and lesbian relationship.
She and her partner suffered verbal abuse, neighbour harassment, job loss, and a violent attack in Prague; police allegedly failed to investigate.
The adjudicator and IAT rejected asylum and human rights claims; limited permission to appeal was granted on Article 8 only.
Counsel later accepted the appeal could not succeed but the appellant did not instruct withdrawal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal against an IAT decision dismissing an asylum and human rights appeal; renewed application for permission on other grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; renewed application for permission refused.
enrichment.ratio: Following Ullah, where treatment in the receiving state is not severe enough to engage Article 3, English courts are not required to treat other Convention articles as engaged by prospective treatment abroad; on the facts the Czech state had not failed to secure effective respect for private life.
legal_issues: Whether expulsion engaging Article 8 by reason of treatment in the destination state survives Ullah
Whether ill-treatment amounted to persecution or Article 3 degrading treatment
Whether the Czech authorities were unable or unwilling to protect against non-state agent violence

enrichment.short_title: Lawfulness of arrest for offensive weapon in public place
key_facts: PC Pickthall arrested Keith Mossop in the street after receiving reports of threats with a hammer at Friars Close.
Mossop pleaded guilty to two counts of resisting arrest after magistrates rejected a no-case submission.
The defence argued the officer lacked reasonable grounds to suspect possession of an offensive weapon in a public place.
The justices found reasonable suspicion of an offence at Friars Close but did not address whether all elements of the offence were suspected.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from magistrates' convictions for resisting arrest.
enrichment.ratio: An officer must have reasonable grounds to suspect all elements of an arrestable offence, including that an offensive weapon was carried in a public place; suspicion of conduct at a private address does not alone justify arrest for section 1(4) Prevention of Crime Act 1953, following Chapman v DPP.
legal_issues: Whether reasonable suspicion required proof of all elements of the offence
Whether arrest was lawful so resisting arrest could be proved
Application of Chapman v Director of Public Prosecutions

enrichment.short_title: Scope of PPE maintenance duty after boot hole injury

statutes_considered.title: Personal Protective Equipment at Work Regulations 1992

key_facts: An HGV driver wore employer-supplied steel-capped boots while working in freezing conditions on farms.
An undetectable hole near the toecap let in water and caused frostbite; the toecap itself remained effective.
The recorder found breach under Manual Handling Regulations but not under PPE Regulations or negligence; Astill J allowed the employer's appeal on manual handling.
The Court of Appeal split 2-1 on whether regulation 7(1) imposed absolute liability for the whole boot or only the protective function.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Employee's appeal to the Court of Appeal on construction of regulation 7(1) of the 1992 PPE Regulations.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed by majority; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Although regulation 7(1) imposes an absolute duty, it is concerned with maintaining protective equipment effective against the identified risk; injury from a defect unrelated to that protective function requires proof of common law negligence, not breach of statutory duty.
legal_issues: Construction of 'maintained in efficient working order and in good repair' under regulation 7(1)
Whether absolute maintenance duty covers the whole item of PPE or only the protective element
Ambit of breach of statutory duty where injury is outside the risk the equipment addressed

enrichment.short_title: Nurse back injury causation and Holtby apportionment
key_facts: A charge nurse at Newham General Hospital suffered serious lumbar disc and conus damage after staff shortages forced manual lifting of dependent patients.
The trust accepted pressure on staff but argued constitutional degenerative disease and a bath slip triggered symptoms.
Simon J found breach of manual handling duties and that workplace lifting materially contributed to disc prolapse and neurological injury.
The trust appealed on causation, adequacy of reasons, and apportionment with earlier nursing employments.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Employer's appeal against finding of liability for workplace back and neurological injury.
enrichment.ratio: Where breach of manual handling duties progressively weakened disc annuli leading to a single indivisible prolapse and conus injury, the employer is liable for the whole damage; Holtby time-exposure apportionment does not apply to distinguish earlier non-negligent employment from the catastrophic event.
legal_issues: Causation of disc prolapse and conus compression versus constitutional degeneration
Adequacy of trial judge's reasons under English v Emery Reimbold
Whether liability should be apportioned under Holtby for earlier lifting in other employments

enrichment.short_title: Westminster refusal of Southwark homelessness referral
key_facts: Southwark found Bashir Jbari homeless, in priority need, and not intentionally homeless, then referred him to Westminster under section 198.
Westminster refused the referral in May 2002, citing a notice to quit for tenancy breach and incomplete intentionality enquiries.
Further landlord correspondence showed Jbari had left an intolerable household situation rather than caused nuisance.
The claimant sought judicial review after Westminster failed to secure interim accommodation under section 200.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Westminster's refusal to accept a section 198 homelessness referral from Southwark.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; Westminster ordered to determine the application in compliance with Part VII of the Housing Act 1996.
enrichment.ratio: A notified authority cannot reject a section 198 referral by challenging the notifying authority's section 193 decision without timely judicial review; once Southwark lawfully found no intentional homelessness, Westminster was bound to accept referral duties under section 200.
legal_issues: Whether Westminster could refuse a referral without quashing Southwark's section 193 decision
Intentionality where a notice to quit cited tenancy breach
Whether a notifying authority may revisit a favourable homelessness decision absent fraud or changed circumstances

enrichment.short_title: Defendant's costs order after waste prosecution dismissed
key_facts: The Environment Agency prosecuted Harry A Coff Ltd and Michael Coff for unlicensed waste deposit at Sandford Farm.
Prosecution against the company was dismissed on 4 July 2002 when no evidence was offered; Michael Coff later pleaded guilty.
The company applied for a defendant's costs order from central funds; the district judge refused, inferring the company and Michael Coff were effectively the same.
Counsel agreed the judge erred in refusing any order and in findings unsupported by evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated against refusal of a magistrates' court defendant's costs order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; defendant's costs order substituted for assessment without remittal.
enrichment.ratio: A magistrates' court should normally grant a defendant's costs order where prosecution is dismissed and cannot refuse one outright because of the quantum initially mentioned; unsupported findings that a corporate defendant was the directing mind of an individual co-defendant cannot justify denial of central funds costs.
legal_issues: When a defendant's costs order must be made under section 16
Whether refusal for excessive claimed amount was lawful before assessment
Evidential basis for treating company and individual defendant as identical

confidence.notes: Clear statutory analysis with agreed facts on what occurred before the district judge.

key_facts: Fisher bought property adjacent to plot 7 from MW Developments Ltd in 1985 with a 20-year pre-emption if planning permission was not obtained.
The pre-emption was misregistered as affecting Oxfordshire land though plot 7 was in Buckinghamshire.
In 1991 Mr Merer transferred plot 7 to his wife for a stated £80,000 without money passing; Fisher discovered the transfer in 1999.
The judge held Mrs Merer was not a purchaser for money or money's worth and ordered specific performance at £11,000.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Chancery Division trial declaring an unregistered pre-emption binding and ordering transfer at a fixed price.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on consideration issue; allowed on remedy; specific performance ordered on contractual terms without substituted valuation.
enrichment.ratio: Where an unregistered estate contract binds because the transferee gave no consideration, specific performance follows the contract machinery; the court should not substitute a joint expert valuation for the contractual offer-and-valuer process while the contractual machinery remains available.
legal_issues: Whether Mrs Merer was a purchaser for money or money's worth under section 4(6)
Whether consideration was satisfied by debt write-off to her husband
Whether Sudbrook permits court-imposed valuation without failure of contractual machinery

enrichment.short_title: Extended sentence for unprovoked fatal assault
key_facts: A 17-year-old pleaded guilty to manslaughter after an indictment for murder; Luke Richmond, 16, died from head injuries after an unprovoked attack.
The appellant punched Richmond twice, causing a fatal fall, then kicked him hard in the head while he lay on the ground.
Judge Pollard imposed an extended sentence of 8 years: 6 years custody plus 2 years extension.
The victim's family had no warning when the manslaughter plea was accepted at a listing hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Sentence appeal by leave against an extended sentence for manslaughter.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; 2-year extension period quashed; 6-year custodial term upheld.
enrichment.ratio: For unprovoked street violence against an innocent victim, a six-year custodial term for manslaughter can fall within the acceptable range; an extended licence period under section 85 is unnecessary for a young first offender where normal licence suffices.
legal_issues: Appropriate custodial length for unprovoked manslaughter by punch and kick
Whether post-fatal kick is an aggravating feature
Whether a section 85 extension period was warranted

enrichment.short_title: Footballer's disability claim barred by five games
key_facts: David Howells, a Southampton Premier League footballer, injured his knee in October 1998 and later suffered further symptoms in July 1999.
He played eight reserve-team competitive matches between October and December 1999 during a claimed 12-month total disablement period.
Southampton told him in December 1999 he would not return to the first team and he retired as a professional footballer.
IGI Insurance applied for summary judgment, relying on claim condition 11 deeming five or more games conclusive proof of full rehabilitation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from summary judgment under CPR Part 24 dismissing a permanent total disablement insurance claim.
enrichment.ratio: In a professional sports disability policy insuring the occupation of 'professional footballer', claim condition 11 treats any five competitive professional club games within the relevant disablement period as conclusive rehabilitation, including reserve-team matches, regardless of rehabilitative purpose or prior playing level.
legal_issues: Construction of undefined 'games' in claim condition 11
Whether reserve-team appearances count toward the five-game threshold
Whether playing level before injury limits the meaning of 'game'

enrichment.short_title: Shotgun certificate renewal and Hampshire residence
key_facts: Huw Mills-Owens applied to Hampshire Constabulary to renew a shotgun certificate for Westwood, Ringwood.
Police inquiries and photographs indicated the property was neglected with no signs of regular occupation.
Mills-Owens also had addresses in Chiswick and Chesham Street and visited Westwood only occasionally.
The Crown Court upheld refusal; no challenge to his suitability to hold firearms, only residence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from Crown Court dismissal of appeal against refusal to renew a shotgun certificate.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; questions on construction and evidence answered in the affirmative.
enrichment.ratio: Section 26(1) requires application to the chief officer for the area in which the applicant resides; residence is a factual question and sporadic visits without regular occupation evidence do not satisfy the statutory requirement, following Burditt v Joslin.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'resides' under section 26(1) Firearms Act 1968
Whether multiple homes can establish residence in the licensing area
Whether evidence supported the chief constable's jurisdictional refusal
